faqs.a: A common rule is to contribute at least enough to get the full employer match, since that is an instant return of 50 to 100 percent. Many advisors then suggest working toward 10 to 15 percent of salary including the match.
faqs.q: How much should I contribute to my 401(k)?

faqs.a: It is money your employer adds to your account based on what you contribute. A typical formula is 50 cents for every dollar you contribute, up to 6 percent of your salary. If you contribute less than that threshold, you leave free money behind.

US stocks have returned roughly 7 percent per year after inflation over long periods, but that is backward-looking and not guaranteed. A diversified portfolio might use 5 to 7 percent nominal; this calculator asks you to pick and shows how sensitive the result is.
Essentially, yes, once it is vested. Some employers require you to stay a certain number of years before their contributions fully become yours. Check your plan's vesting schedule.
faqs.q: Is the match really free money?

faqs.a: Withdrawals before age 59 and a half usually incur income tax plus a 10 percent penalty, with limited hardship exceptions. The calculator assumes you leave the money invested until retirement.
faqs.q: Can I withdraw from a 401(k) early?

faqs.a: The growth math is the same; only the tax treatment differs. Roth contributions are made after tax and withdrawn tax-free in retirement, while traditional contributions are pre-tax. This tool models the balance, not the tax.
faqs.q: Does this calculator handle Roth 401(k) contributions?

keyFacts: A 401(k) is an employer-sponsored retirement account in the United States where contributions are deducted from your paycheck before tax.
Many employers match a portion of what you contribute, for example 50% of your contributions up to 6% of your salary. That match is free money.
Contributions grow tax-deferred; you generally pay tax only when you withdraw in retirement, usually after age 59 and a half.
Annual contribution limits are set by the IRS and change most years; employees aged 50 and over can make extra catch-up contributions.
Compounding means the single biggest lever is time: starting ten years earlier can matter more than contributing ten percent more.

401k-calculator.quickAnswer: A 401(k) calculator projects your retirement balance by compounding your contributions plus your employer's matching contributions at your expected annual return. With a $25,000 balance, 6% of a $75,000 salary, a 50% employer match and 7% returns over 30 years, you could reach about $828,000.
401k-calculator.tagline: Project your 401(k) retirement savings with employer matching.
401k-calculator.workedExample:
Salary $75,000, you contribute 6% ($4,500/year), employer matches 50% of contributions up to 6% of salary ($2,250/year). Starting balance $25,000, return 7%, horizon 30 years.

(1.07)^30 = 7.61225. Balance part: 25,000 x 7.61225 = $190,306. Annual contributions of $6,750: factor = (7.61225 - 1) / 0.07 = 94.4607, so 6,750 x 94.4607 = $637,610. Projected total = $827,916.

Of that, you contributed $135,000, your employer added $67,500, and $600,416 came from growth.
